hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something good you’re part of that you might never see finished?
options: then this old man is your friend. listen.
then you’ll understand his tears. listen.
then let this one plant the thought. listen.

steps.line: High in the mountains lived an old sage named Asita. One day, the story says, he saw the gods celebrating. “A child is born,” they said, “who will wake up.”
Asita hurried down to the palace. The Sakyans showed him the baby prince, and the old man took him in his arms.
He looked closely, the way an expert looks at something rare, and his face lit up. “This one is supreme,” he said, “the highest among people.”

steps.q: Then, still holding the child, the old man starts to cry. Why do you think?
o: He sees danger coming for the boy
He’s sad the boy will one day leave home
steps.why: Not for the child. For himself: he’s old, and this boy’s teaching is still decades away.

steps.line: The family was frightened. “Is the child in danger?” “No,” said Asita. “I weep for myself. I am old. I’ll be gone before he teaches, and never hear it.”

steps.q: Asita is a holy man, near the end of a long life. Why is missing this child’s teaching such a loss to him?
o: He’d sought that truth his whole life
He’d lose the honor of having known the boy
He’d hoped to be the boy’s own teacher
steps.why: In the poem Asita is a lifelong seeker. To meet the one who will find the way, too late to walk it with him, is the sharpest kind of grief.

steps.line: So he went to his young nephew, Nalaka. “When you hear that someone has woken up and is teaching,” he said, “go to him.” Years later, Nalaka did.

steps.q: Years later, Nalaka did find the Buddha. What did he ask him about?
o: Whether his uncle had seen truly
Where his uncle had been reborn
How to live as a true sage
steps.why: The Buddha answered with the way of the silent sage, and a picture: small streams run noisy, the great river flows quiet.

steps.q: In later tellings, eight wise men read the baby’s marks. Seven said: a world-ruling king, or a Buddha. What did the youngest say?
o: Only a Buddha, no doubt at all
He refused to make a guess
steps.why: His name was Kondañña. Years later he was the first to understand the Buddha’s very first teaching.

steps.line: Today, an old woman plants a tree whose shade she won’t sit in. A teacher believes in a kid she won’t see grown.
steps.label: today

say: this story is told in verse, in one of the oldest parts of the buddhist scriptures. it’s a strange, tender moment this early on: the one who sees most clearly who this child is knows he will never see it come true.

every tradition keeps asita. later tellings, in theravada and mahayana lives of the buddha alike, add that he read thirty-two marks of a great person on the baby’s body. the scene was carved in stone in ancient gandhara, in today’s pakistan and afghanistan.

steps.q: Asita grieved, and still sent Nalaka. What does the story suggest about a good thing you won’t see finished?
o: Plant it anyway, for someone else
Don’t start what you can’t finish
Grieve it, and let it go
steps.why: His joy and his grief were both real. He let the joy do something.

today.say: today, do one good thing you won’t see finished: a note to a young person, a seed in a pot, a small gift to a cause that will outlive you. plant it anyway.
options: then thank you. it counts, even unseen.

sources: Nalaka Sutta (Sutta Nipata 3.11), introductory verses: Asita sees the gods of the Thirty-three rejoicing; goes to Suddhodana’s house; holds the child, examines him, proclaims him supreme; weeps; reassures the Sakyans that no harm will come to the child; grieves that his own life will end before the teaching; instructs his nephew Nalaka
Lakkhana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 30): the thirty-two marks; Nidanakatha (Asita’s visit)
Gandhara reliefs of Asita holding the infant
check: The text has Asita seeing the gods during his daytime rest; “high in the mountains” is a gentle simplification.
